the_finding_that_reorders_everything:
The first ranking scored the candidates on demand, local phrasing and source coverage, and put en-AU first, tr-TR second, id-ID third and es-MX fourth. ko-KR was not in it at all. Reading the SERPs changed the order almost completely, because the two candidates with the LARGEST measured demand have the WORST SERPs and the two with the most open SERPs are the two that need no new language.

  ko-KR  250,330 measured volume  - five of five SERPs owned by Naver and official boards
  id-ID   49,330 measured volume  - every organic slot held by Klook, Trip.com, Traveloka
  en-AU   50,000 measured volume  - two DOMAIN RATING 4 sites in the top five
  es-MX   31,050 measured volume  - a DOMAIN RATING 16 site at position 3
  tr-TR  ~190,000 measured volume - a DOMAIN RATING 2 site at position 3 on the region family, a DR 16 at 6 on the city family, state portals on the entity family

Demand says which markets are worth wanting. The SERP says which of them are reachable. Ranking on demand alone would have put the single least reachable market first.

the_six_criteria_the_brief_names_and_whe.1_search_demand_total: ko-KR 250,330, tr-TR ~190,000, en-AU 50,000, id-ID 49,330, es-MX 31,050. This criterion alone ranks the two unreachable markets first and second.
the_six_criteria_the_brief_names_and_whe.2_local_language_opportunity: every candidate passed. Turkish, Korean and Indonesian phrasing was measured in the language, not translated: gezilecek yerler, yeohaeng, tempat wisata. en-AU and es-MX need no new phrasing at all.
the_six_criteria_the_brief_names_and_whe.3_destination_demand: tr-TR earns eleven destination countries of eighteen tested and five of them are captured. ko-KR earns twelve of sixteen and six are captured. Both tables are in their own dated files.
the_six_criteria_the_brief_names_and_whe.4_data_and_source_coverage: tr-TR captured in full. en-AU extracting now. es-MX and id-ID queued. ko-KR not queued at all.
the_six_criteria_the_brief_names_and_whe.5_expected_valid_page_yield: measured by rebuild for tr-TR rather than estimated. For the others the only honest anchor is en-GB contributing 34,980 /en/ URLs that en-US does not claim, and that anchor is quoted rather than extrapolated into a number.
the_six_criteria_the_brief_names_and_whe.6_low_duplicate_risk: measured, not assumed. Distinct /en/ URLs equals rows per language exactly (en-GB 34,980 + en-US 49,299 = 84,279), so a second market in one language adds pages for entities the others do not search. That is why en-AU and es-MX pay and de-AT, which would search the same Austrian entities de-DE already reaches, does not.

what_is_being_built_and_in_what_order: 1. tr-TR, materialised 2026-10-05. Home country already on disk, so it was the only candidate that could be built the day it was measured.
2. en-AU, as soon as the Australian layers finish. Best SERP of any candidate, no new language, and the entities are ones no existing market searches.
3. es-MX, as soon as Mexico is captured. Same shape as en-AU, smaller.

4. id-ID and ko-KR: NOT built. Measured, recorded, deprioritised on the SERP, and left wired so that admitting either is one line in MARKETS if the SERP question is ever answered differently. Indonesia is still being captured, as a DESTINATION for the existing markets.
what_would_change_the_two_refusals: Neither is a gate relaxation. For ko-KR: a Korean family whose SERP is open that was not among the five sampled, or a Naver-first distribution strategy that Google organic ranking is the wrong test for, or South Korea captured and a domestic family measuring open. For id-ID: the same, a family outside the OTA-held city-guide shape. Until then, both would be pages built to rank behind a platform, and tens of thousands of them would add template mass to a site whose whole defence is that every page earns its place.

the_structural_fact_that_shapes_this_who: Every URL in the manifest belongs to exactly ONE market, and distinct URLs per language equals rows per language exactly: en-GB holds 34,980 and en-US 49,299, together exactly the 84,279 distinct /en/ URLs. So the two English markets do not duplicate each other, they contribute DIFFERENT entities to a shared language space. That means a new market pays off in two different ways and they have to be ranked differently. A new LANGUAGE opens a new URL space and needs a new alternate-name pass, a new sitelink language and new local phrasing. A new MARKET IN AN EXISTING LANGUAGE needs none of that and still adds pages, but only for the entities the existing markets do not already search, which is exactly what separates en-AU from de-AT.
